scenes.title: The lordship of the manor
scenes.narration: Llandough belongs to Tewkesbury Abbey until the Dissolution of 1536–39. Cardiff Records states that in 1543 Henry VIII granted the manor to Lord Clynton and Say and Robert Turwitt, and that by 1545 it was held by Sir George Herbert. The Western Mail letter says the Herberts held the lordship until the Earl of Bute bought it in 1793; Cardiff Records places William Hurst and others in the account from 1767. The same 1974 newspaper record identifies Mary Williams's family as occupying the manorial home since 1667. That occupation and the lordship are separate from the farmhouse freehold. The family's case is that the Williamses were virtual freeholders under the 1877 bargain while quarrying continued, and that Parcel A's freehold passed to them in 1928 when quarrying ended.

scenes.received: The lord of the manor owned the farm.

scenes.known: Lordship of a manor and ownership of the farmhouse parcel are separate interests. The 1974 newspaper records the Williams family’s occupation of the manorial home since 1667. The family’s title case is not occupation alone: it is that the 1877 bargain entitled the Williamses to Parcel A’s freehold when quarrying ended, identified by Mary as 1928, when the final rent was paid. On that account, the Williamses were virtual freeholders while the quarrying arrangement ran and became freeholders in 1928. The 1877 deed and final receipt have not been located, so the 1928 transfer remains the family’s asserted title history rather than a fact determined by the 1974 newspaper or a court. The manorial sources also differ over 1767–1793; the Herbert estate papers have not yet been checked.

scenes.title: A 1,000-year lease of Cydwin
scenes.narration: The National Library of Wales catalogue describes a lease for 1,000 years dated 20 June 1547 from Sir George Herbert of Swansea to Edmund Vaughan of a farm called Cydwin in the manor of Llandough; the record names fields. This long leasehold interest predates the later Bute estate narrative. The affirmative Cedwyn thesis asks whether those named fields belong to the older Cydfin/Ty Mawr holding later catalogued as a 107-acre farm, and how that interest passed from the Herbert/Vaughan line into subsequent estate records. The instrument and field boundaries must be examined before the lease can be equated with the whole Great House site.

questions.question: When did the Williams family come to Great House, and on what terms?
questions.answer: The 1667 date rests on Mary Williams's c. 1974 statement and the 1974 press reports that repeat it. No document of 1667 has been found. The family's own correspondence describes 1667 three ways: a purchase, continuous occupation 'since at least 1667', and a lease for 999 years. The heritage record (Suggett 1988, GGAT02038s) says the Vaughans, a minor gentry family, occupied Great House as the chief freehold farm from the mid-16th to the late 18th century. Both can be true only if the Williamses held under the Vaughans (as tenants or lessees) before the Bute purchase.

scenes.title: The Bute Estate
scenes.narration: The historical account places Bute's acquisition of the lordship of Llandough in 1793 and its acquisition of the Great House freehold in the early 19th century; the manorial courts of Llandough and Leckwith were held at the house. scenes.known: Parcel A was the family's from 1928, and by possession from 1940. It was never shown to belong to Western Ground Rents or BP. A synthetic single farm was described in 1916; six attempts (1949, 1955, 1959, 1962, 1965, 1974) treated Mary's occupation as permissive; the woodland and the land to the south were taken; the 1975 conveyance and 1983 registration gave the synthetic Parcel A a deed and a title; the 1987 amalgamation folded it into Parcel B. The courts decided possession and never decided ownership. Possession can be awarded without ownership being tried, and land can be registered without a rival claim being decided. Neither decides the older title.

case_questions.question: When did the Williams family come to Great House, and on what terms?
case_questions.answer: The 1667 date rests on Mary Williams's c. 1974 statement and the 1974 press reports that repeat it. No document of 1667 has been found. The family's own correspondence describes 1667 three ways: a purchase, continuous occupation 'since at least 1667', and a lease for 999 years. The heritage record (Suggett 1988, GGAT02038s) says the Vaughans, a minor gentry family, occupied Great House as the chief freehold farm from the mid-16th to the late 18th century. Both can be true only if the Williamses held under the Vaughans (as tenants or lessees) before the Bute purchase.
for: Mary Williams's statement (c. 1974)
1974 newspaper reports
Family tradition of nine generations
Western Mail, 20 November 1958 (snippet only): Mrs M. D. Buckler tells the county planning committee the land was "farmed by her family since 1667"
against: RCAHMW Archive 6048945 / Heneb GGAT02038s: Vaughans occupied the house mid-C16 to late C18
No 1667 deed, lease, court roll entry or fine located in any archive searched
next: 1670 Glamorgan hearth tax (published, Welsh Journals Online): who was the householder at Great House?

case_questions.question: When and how did the Bute Estate acquire Great House from the Vaughans?
case_questions.answer: Bute bought the lordship of the manor in 1793. The heritage record says Bute acquired the freehold of Great House in the early 19th century. The conveyance from the Vaughans or their heirs has not been located, so the date, the price and any leases it recited are unknown.
for: Heneb GGAT02038s / RCAHMW Archive 6048945: 'In the early C19 the freehold was acquired by the Bute Estate'

case_questions.question: What happened in 1877: did Bute sell the farmhouse and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas, or only lease quarrying rights?
case_questions.answer: Mary's statement says Bute sold the farmhouse, buildings and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas in 1877 and kept about 9 acres, with the house to pass to the Williamses when quarrying ended. No deed has been found. Glamorgan Archives found no deeds for an 1877 Daniel Thomas transaction (2026/4097b) and pointed to Bute X.6(12), the Bute trustees' 1877 abstract of payments and receipts at Cardiff Library. DBDT/79/1, a May 1877 lease to a John Williams, was examined and is a Pembroke Terrace, Cardiff property, not Llandough (2026/3893). A capital receipt from Daniel Thomas in Bute X.6(12) would point to a sale; a rent or royalty would point to a lease.
for: Mary Williams's statement (c. 1974)
Western Ground Rents and BP later dealt with the farmhouse and garden as a separate unit (1959, 1962, 1965, 1975, 1983)
against: No 1877 deed located at Glamorgan Archives (2026/4097b)
NLW FOI/2026/09 searches of Bute series D153 and D205 did not produce it

case_questions.question: Is the 1881 census's "Llandough Home Farm" Great House Farm?
case_questions.answer: Very probably, on who lived there; not on the name. The census household (RG11/5288 p.2, schedule 9) is John Williams, 53, farmer, born at Leckwith. Directories of 1868, 1875 and 1880, and of 1887, 1891 and 1901, list "Williams John, Great house" / "Great House farm, Llandough", and list the Rees family separately at Llandough Farm. The South Wales Star of 1892 has "Mr. John Williams, Great House Farm, Llandough". Per Sion Buckler, the census entered Great House Farm under the wrong name. No other source uses "Home Farm".

case_questions.answer: The order was against Frederick Buckler, described as 'the whole of the farm'. Possession was taken on 4 July 1955 of everything except the farmhouse and garden. Mary was not a party. The 1987 court counted adverse possession of the house from 1955.

case_questions.question: Was the farm's water cut off, when, by whom, and why?
case_questions.answer: Mrs M. D. Buckler (Mary Williams) told Glamorgan County Council's planning committee in November 1958 that "the water was cut off from her house and grounds for nearly 10 years by order of Western Ground Rents" (Western Mail, 20 November 1958, snippet only). Per Branwen Buckler (voice testimony), the council cut it over bills that Mary (Nancy) Williams insisted were paid, cattle drowned in the River Ely trying to reach water, and it was raised in Parliament. In the 1950s Llandough was in Penarth Urban District; Cardiff Corporation was the public water undertaker for the area, and in 1914 the Bute estate also supplied part of Penarth Urban District from a private spring at Llandough.

case_questions.question: What did the courts actually decide in 1986–88: ownership, or only possession?
case_questions.answer: The Court of Appeal decided a claim for possession and a defence of adverse possession: it found adverse possession from 1955 but held time was stopped by the 1962 action and the 1974 letters made the occupation permissive. It did not try Mary's 1974 ownership plea. The House of Lords refused leave in March 1988; its judicial papers are YHL/PO/JO/10/11/2536 at TNA, catalogued only on 20 May 2026.
